questions.prompt: Which task is the best LoRA candidate?
questions.explain: A narrow, repeatable task with examples with known answers and a clear right answer can be tuned and measured. Open-ended or one-off tasks lack that.

options.text: Tagging 3,000 hand-marked notes with one of five fixed categories
Writing a new discussion section for each manuscript
options.misconception: Open-ended writing has no single right answer and no clean labels, so you cannot show a tuned model is better.

options.text: Answering questions about a hosted model's API that you cannot download
options.misconception: LoRA needs the model weights. A hosted model reached through an API usually does not give them to you.

options.text: Finding a typo in one file today
options.misconception: A one-off job has no repeatable pattern and no examples to train on.

questions.prompt: Sort each item by whether it is one of the four conditions for LoRA or something else.
questions.explain: The four conditions are weights, a narrow repeatable task, examples with known answers with some held back, and an eval against the untuned model.

items.text: You can download the model's weights
items.misconception: Training adapters on frozen weights needs the weights themselves.

items.text: Examples with known answers, some held back for testing
items.misconception: Held-back examples are what let you test the tuned model fairly.

items.text: An eval that shows the tuned model beats the untuned one
items.misconception: Without an eval you cannot tell whether tuning helped.

items.text: The model is the largest one on offer
items.misconception: Size is not one of the four conditions. A narrow task can suit a small open-weight model.

items.text: You have never tried changing the prompt
items.misconception: Trying a clearer prompt first is advice. Having not tried it is not a reason to tune.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order you try them when an agent does a job badly.
questions.explain: Cheap, reversible changes come first. Fine-tuning comes last and only after a working eval shows the earlier steps fell short.
items: Write a working eval that measures the job
Make the prompt clearer and re-run the eval
Give the agent better tools and re-run the eval
Consider fine-tuning if the eval shows the gap remains on a narrow task

questions.prompt: Match each thing to what it is in LoRA fine-tuning.
questions.explain: The base weights are frozen, the adapter is trained, the merge folds the adapter in, and the eval checks the result.

pairs.right: Frozen: they stay as they are
pairs.misconception: LoRA leaves the original weights unchanged and trains something small beside them.

pairs.right: Small extra parts that are trained
pairs.misconception: The adapter is the new, trained piece. The base is the frozen one.

pairs.right: Folds the adapter into the base model afterwards
pairs.misconception: Merging happens after training and combines the pieces. It is not the training step.

pairs.right: Used to test the tuned model
pairs.misconception: Training examples teach the model. Held-back ones check it.

questions.prompt: A student plans to fine-tune a model for masking sample IDs. Which line is the risky one?
questions.explain: The tuned model has to be compared with the untuned one on held-back notes. Judging it on the notes it trained on hides failures.

lines.text: 1. Check that I can download the open-weight model.
lines.why: Having the weights is the first condition.
Held-back notes make a fair test possible.

lines.text: 3. Test the tuned model on the same notes it was trained on, and call it done.
4. Record the training data, adapter version and base model.
lines.why: The adapter belongs to its base model and its data, so all three are tracked.
